Oof, that is incredibly frustrating, especially when the other pieces on the bed printed perfectly.

Looking at the image, your diagnosis is spot-on. What you're seeing on that large, curved piece is a classic case of mechanical leverage failure. As the print gets taller, any slight upward curling or warping acts like a lever. When the nozzle travels across that "wave" or gyroid-style infill pattern, it can strike a slightly raised edge. Because the part is tall, that small horizontal impact exerts a massive amount of torque at the base, snapping the top layers loose or breaking the bed adhesion entirely.

Here is a breakdown of why this specific piece failed while the others survived, and how to prevent it on the next run.

Why Did This Specific Piece Fail?

  • The Geometry Trapped Heat: The long, thin, curved wall acts like a chimney. Heat from the bed and the nozzle gets trapped inside the curve, causing the plastic to cool unevenly. This uneven cooling causes the top edges to curl upward slightly.
  • The Travel Path Crux: Unlike the neat, compact cylinders next to it, the print head has to make long, sweeping movements across this curved piece. If it hits an area where the infill or perimeter has curled up even a fraction of a millimeter, it acts like a speed bump at high speed.
  • Infill Impact: Certain infill patterns (like Grid or Triangle) cross over themselves on the same layer, creating tiny vertical high spots. While gyroid usually avoids this, a high-flow wave pattern can still suffer from slight over-extrusion at the turnarounds, leaving a ridge for the nozzle to catch.

How to Fix It for the Next Print

To get this piece across the finish line, you'll want to focus on reducing nozzle collisions and managing thermal stress.

1. Enable Z-Hop (The Easiest Fix)

If you don't have Z-Hop enabled, turn it on in your slicer.

  • Set a Z-Hop Height of 0.2mm to 0.4mm.
  • This forces the toolhead to lift vertically before making a travel move across the print, entirely eliminating the chance of it hitting a curled edge while moving between points.

2. Change Your Infill Pattern

If the current pattern is creating high spots or causing vibration when the nozzle sweeps across it:

  • Switch to Gyroid (if you aren't already using it) or Cross 3D. Gyroid doesn't cross its own path on a single layer, which drastically minimizes nozzle scraping.

3. Manage the Cooling & Speed

Because that curved wall is prone to warping upward:

  • Slow down the outer wall speed and the infill speed for this specific part (or the whole layer height where it failed). Less speed means less mechanical force if a minor collision does happen.
  • Slightly increase your cooling fan min/max times for short layers to give the plastic a chance to fully solidify before the nozzle comes back around.

4. Orient for Success

If you have to reprint just this piece, try rotating it 90 degrees on the build plate. Sometimes aligning the long curves with the direction of the bed's movement (or the toolhead's primary axis) reduces the harshness of sudden directional changes and improves cooling.
